entities.name: Aymer de Lusignan
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Aymer de Lusignan, also known as Aymer de Valence, was a pivotal ecclesiastical and political figure in 13th-century England, serving as Bishop-elect of Winchester from 1250 until his death in 1260. Born into the powerful Lusignan dynasty, a prominent French noble family, and half-brother to King Henry III of England through his mother Isabella of Angoulême, Aymer's rapid rise to power and wealth exemplified the controversial influence of foreign 'Poitevin' relatives at the English court. His appointment to one of England's richest sees, despite lacking canonical qualifications and being underage, ignited significant resentment among the English baronage and native clergy, contributing directly to the volatile political climate that culminated in the Provisions of Oxford in 1258.

His tenure as bishop-elect was marked by continuous conflict and a notable absence from his diocese. Despite papal dispensations and royal backing, Aymer's attempts to assert control over the cathedral chapter of Winchester were met with fierce resistance, leading to violent confrontations and excommunications. He never received full consecration as bishop, spending much of his time in France and Rome, advocating for his position and securing further ecclesiastical appointments for himself and his kin. His administrative style, characterized by leveraging royal and papal authority to accumulate benefices and wealth, underscored the broader tensions between secular and ecclesiastical power, as well as the growing xenophobia within England's ruling class.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Aymer de Lusignan's controversial appointment and the ensuing conflicts significantly exacerbated tensions between the English Crown and its baronage, directly contributing to the political crisis that led to the Provisions of Oxford and the Second Barons' War, fundamentally reshaping medieval English governance.
